messages.subject: [Rqtl-disc] R/qtl version 1.15-15
messages.body_plain:
A new version of R/qtl (1.15-15) has been released at its web site
(http://www.rqtl.org).  Compiled versions should appear on the R
archive (CRAN) within a couple of days.

The major change: we have incorporated Ritsert Jansen's MQM method
into R/qtl (thanks to Danny Arends and Pjotr Prins).  See the MQM
tutorial at http://www.rqtl.org/tutorials/MQM-tour.pdf

Other changes are listed at http://www.rqtl.org/STATUS.txt

Karl Broman
kbr...@biostat.wisc.edu

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] F2 and BC segregating markers to make a linkage map
messages.body_plain:
hi all!
I am trying to design the linkage map for my organisms since I do not
have one. I have F2 cross but since it was not done from the inbreed
line, there are some markers that are segregating in the normal F2
fashion and the others that are segregating in Back cross fashion,
because the F1 were not  heterozygous for all the markers that were
typed but rather homozygous for one of the F1 for some markers. The
same individuals are typed for all this markers
So treat each group of the markers separately and do all this steps of
estimating rf and do the linkage groups and than join them, or on
which point I can join this data to perform the best map by
integrating this two group of markers into one map?
Thank you!

--

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] F2 and BC segregating markers to make a linkage map
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] F2 and BC segregating markers to make a linkage map
messages.body_plain:
I don't have much experience with this, but here are my initial thoughts:

If you have quite a lot of fully informative markers, you should be able to do everything all at once.

If there are just a few fully informative markers, you should probably work with the two groups of backcross-type markers separately, but including all fully informative ones in each, and then look to see whether you can merge the two maps afterwards.  You'd need at least two fully informative markers on a linkage group, and it'd be best if you had more, in order to merge the two groups of markers into one map.

karl
-----------
Karl Broman
kbr...@biostat.wisc.edu
http://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman

messages.subject: [Rqtl-disc] two-qtl scan thresholds
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I am interested in running two-qtl scans for traits in plants (eg
tomato). You recommend some pre-determined threshold levels
(calculated based on simulations of crosses) for mouse BC2 and F2
populations in your book, considering the 10's of hours and computer
resources it takes to compute for any reasonable number of
permutations.

Do you have any threshold suggestions for two-qtl scans (for all the
models) for plant (quantitative) traits in BC and F2 populations?

Thanks,
Isaak

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Estimated QTL effects with CIM in RIL
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Estimated QTL effects with CIM in RIL
messages.body_plain:
For a backcross, the estimated additive effect for a QTL in fitqtl() is the estimated difference between the average phenotype for the heterozygote and that for the homozygote.  Basically we code the two genotypes as +/- 0.5 and then do linear regression.

For RIL, it should be half the difference between the two homozygotes, but it looks like it's currently giving just the difference between the two homozygotes.  I'd call that a bug.

The interaction effects are what you get when you multiply the two QTL genotype columns together.   You then can see that the 2x problem in the additive effect leads to a 4x bug in the interactive effect.  It's supposed to be the difference in the additive effects at one QTL when you consider separately the two genotypes at the other QTL.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] two-qtl scan thresholds
messages.body_plain:
At the moment, there's not really any way to get around either doing a permutation test or some sort of simulation study, to get at thresholds for scantwo().

If you use Haley-Knott regression, that would speed things up considerably.  Also you could use a rather coarse step size, which would give you conservative but still useful thresholds.

karl

messages.subject: [Rqtl-disc] Question about proper model (selection)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a question about model selection:

A one-dimensional, one QTL scan of a trait of interest provided me
with no overwhelming evidence for a QTL; the best supported QTL had a
LOD score of 2.218 with an (from 10,000 permutations) estimated p-
value of 0.0673.

A two-dimensional, two-QTL scan, on the other hand, clearly supported
(at least, that's how I interpreted the data) an additive two-QTL
model with LOD 4.884 and an (from 10,000 permutations) estimated p
value of 0.0087:

      pos1f pos2f lod.full  pval lod.fv1  pval lod.int <http://lod.int>  pval     pos1a
pos2a lod.add   pval lod.av1   pval
c3:c5    70    22     5.38 0.029   3.163 0.216   0.497 1.000
70    23   4.884 0.0087   2.666 0.0608

Interestingly, though, the comparison of the additive two-QTL model
with the single QTL model did not overwhelmingly favor the two-QTL
model over the one-QTL model (LOD{av1}= 2.666; p = 0.0608).

When using the stepwise function to search for a proper QTL model (and
calculating penalties at a significance level of 0.01), it suggested a
model with no QTL at all. Given the following penalties,

    main    heavy    light
3.011569 4.111203 1.614694

this outcome appears logical to me: a single QTL-model would have
needed a LOD score > 3.012 (= Tm) [but was only 2.218], and an
additive two-QTL model a LOD score > 6.024 (= 2 Tm) [but was only
4.884].

My question: Am I right by considering the stepwise model search as
very conservative and by giving the two-dimensional, two-QTL scan more
credibility (i.e. there are likely two additive QTL) in this
particular case?

I think that I am a little bit puzzled by the fact that the two-
dimensional scan apparently suggests an additive two-QTL model, while
the comparison of the additive two-QTL model with a single QTL model
does not overwhelmingly support the former, and that there is little
support for the latter (the one-QTL model) either. Any thoughts on
that?

Best wishes,
Oliver

--

messages.body_plain:
The penalized LOD score criterion in stepwiseqtl() is conservative, and your interpretations are correct.  You have reasonable evidence for two additive QTL.  If you increase the significance level for the penalties to 0.05, perhaps stepwiseqtl() would also arrive at the model with two QTL.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] QTL mapping with selective genotyping
messages.body_plain:
While we discussed the treatment of selective genotyping for a binary trait in a recent paper (Manichaikul and Broman, Genetics 182:863-874, 2009), our code has not yet been incorporated into R/qtl.

However, if you have multiple affected and unaffected individuals with genotype data, you can detect QTL using the ordinary approach to mapping loci for binary traits, ignoring the selective genotyping: scanone() with model="binary".

If you have genotypes only on affected individuals, you're only option is to look for deviations from normal segregation at the genetic markers (1:2:1 in an intercross and 1:1 in a backcross), with geno.table().

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] R/qtl version 1.16-6
messages.body_plain:
There's not really a function to convert between a genetic and physical map.  And there can't be such a function, as there is never a simple relationship between genetic and physical maps.

Rather, there have been some users who've run into trouble with running out of memory in calc.genoprob(), and this has largely turned out to be a case of them having included marker positions in basepairs rather than cM, so that if calc.genoprob is run with step=1, it will attempt to calculate the QTL genotype probabilities at millions of positions.  rescalemap() was added to simply rescale the genetic map in a cross by a factor of 10^-6, to get things into Mbp, though we'd really recommend running est.map() and replace.map() to get an estimated genetic map for later analyses.

karl
